study.briefTitle: Osimertinib in Treating Participants With Stage I-IIIA EGFR-mutant Non-small Cell Lung Cancer Before Surgery

criteria.text: Males and females >=18 years of age
Histologically or cytologically confirmed non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC), performed on a biopsy that occurred within the last 90 days.
Documented activating EGFR mutation (Exon 19 deletion, T790M, or L858R) on tumor samples by Clinical Laboratory Clinical Laboratory Improvement Amendments (CLIA)-approved test
received no more than 28 days of treatment
no evidence of grade 2 or greater treatment adverse events possibly related to treatment with the EGFR TKI
Positron emission tomography (PET)-computed tomography (CT) within the last 60 days showing radiographic stage I to IIIa lung cancer (mediastinal staging biopsy is allowed but not required)
Brain magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) (or CT if contraindication to MRI) within the last 60 days showing no evidence of metastatic disease
Documentation that the patient is a candidate for surgical resection of their lung cancer by an American Board of Thoracic Surgery certified surgeon
The patient must have a tumor size >=1 centimeter (cm) in its longest diameter.
Eastern Cooperative Oncology Group (ECOG) Performance Status (PS) of 0-1

Any unresolved toxicities from prior therapy greater than Common Terminology Criteria for Adverse Events (CTCAE) grade 1 at the time of starting study treatment, with the exception of alopecia and grade 2 prior platinumtherapy-related neuropathy is allowed
Aspartate aminotransferase (AST) and alanine aminotransferase (ALT) =< 2.5 x upper limit of normal (ULN)

Bilirubin =< 1.5 x ULN, (Patients with documented Gilbert's syndrome and conjugated bilirubin within the normal range may be allowed into the study; in this event, it will be documented that the patient was eligible based on conjugated bilirubin levels)
Potassium and magnesium within normal range, patients may receive supplements to meet this requirement
Leukocytes > 3,000/microliter (mcL)
Hemoglobin >= 9 g/dL, with no blood transfusions in the 28 days prior to study entry
Absolute neutrophil count > 1,500/mcL
Platelets > 100,000/mcL
Creatinine Clearance (CrCl) > 50 mL/min for patients with serum creatinine (SCr) > 1.5 x upper limit of normal (ULN)
Ability to swallow oral medications
must have a negative serum pregnancy test within 3 days prior to the first dose of study treatment
agree to use highly effective contraception, during the study and for 90 days following the last dose of osimertinib
Women of childbearing potential (WoCBP): women between menarche and menopause who have not been permanently or surgically sterilized and are capable of procreation
Women NOT of childbearing potential: women who are permanently or surgically sterilized or postmenopausal

Permanent sterilization includes hysterectomy and/or bilateral oophorectomy and/or bilateral salpingectomy but excludes bilateral tubal occlusion; tubal occlusion is considered a highly effective method of birth control but does not absolutely exclude possibility of pregnancy; (the term occlusion refers to both occluding and ligating techniques that do not physically remove the oviducts)
Women who have undergone tubal occlusion should be managed on trials as if they are of WoCBP (e.g. undergo pregnancy testing etc., as required by the study protocol)
Women will be considered postmenopausal if they are amenorrhoeic for 12 months without an alternative medical cause; the following age-specific requirements apply:

Women under 50 years old will be considered postmenopausal if they have been amenorrhoeic for 12 months or more following cessation of exogenous hormonal treatments and with luteinizing hormone and follicle-stimulating hormone levels in the postmenopausal range
Women over 50 years of age will be considered postmenopausal if they have been amenorrhoeic for 12 months or more following cessation of all exogenous hormonal treatments
Acceptable contraception methods are:
Total sexual abstinence (abstinence must be for the total duration of the trial and the follow-up period)
Vasectomized sexual partner plus male condom (with participant assurance that partner received post-vasectomy confirmation of azoospermia)
Tubal occlusion plus male condom
Intra-uterine device - provided coils are copper-banded, plus male condom
Intra-uterine system (IUS) levonorgestrel IUS (e.g., Mirena), plus male condom
Medroxyprogesterone injections (Depo-Provera) plus male condom
Etonogestrel implants (e.g., Implanon, Norplan) plus male condom
Normal and low dose combined oral contraceptive pills, plus male condom
Norelgestromin / ethinylestradiol transdermal system plus male condom
Intravaginal device (e.g., ethinylestradiol and etonogestrel) plus male condom
Cerazette (desogestrel) plus male condom (Cerazette is currently the only highly efficacious progesterone based pill)
Unacceptable Contraception Methods The following methods are considered not to be highly effective and are therefore not acceptable contraceptive methods:
Triphasic combined oral contraceptives
All progesterone only pills except, Cerazette
All barrier methods, if intended to be used alone
Non-copper containing intra-uterine devices
Fertility awareness methods
Coitus interruptus

Men with a female partner of childbearing potential must have either had a prior vasectomy agree to use effective contraception as described in the full protocol for at least 14 days prior to administration of the first dose of study treatment, during the study, and for 90 days following the last dose of osimertinib
Leptomeningeal carcinomatosis or other central nervous system (CNS) metastases

Stage IIIB, or distant metastases (including malignant pleural effusion) identified on PET-CT scan or biopsy (PET abnormalities that are negative for malignancy on biopsy will be considered on a case by case basis

Past medical history of interstitial lung disease, drug-induced interstitial lung disease, radiation pneumonitis which required steroid treatment, or any evidence of clinically active interstitial lung disease
Patients who are known to be serologically positive for human immunodeficiency virus (HIV)

Active second malignancy, i.e. patient known to have potentially fatal cancer present for which he/she may be (but not necessarily) currently receiving treatment; patients with a history of malignancy that has been completely treated, with no evidence of that cancer currently, are permitted to enroll in the trial provided all chemotherapy for prior malignancy was completed > 12 months prior and/or bone marrow transplant > 2 years prior

Patients who are currently receiving treatment with contraindicated corrected QT interval (QTc) prolonging medications or potent CYP3A4 inducers, if that treatment cannot be either discontinued or switched to a different medication prior to first day of study treatment.
Mean resting corrected QT interval (QTc) > 470 msec, obtained from 3 electrocardiograms (ECGs), using the screening clinic ECG machine derived QTc value
Any clinically important abnormalities in rhythm, conduction or morphology of resting ECG e.g. complete left bundle branch block, third degree heart block and second degree heart block

Any factors that increase the risk of QTc prolongation or risk of arrhythmic events such as heart failure, hypokalaemia, congenital long QT syndrome, family history of long QT syndrome or unexplained sudden death under 40 years of age in first degree relatives or any concomitant medication known to prolong the QT interval

Treatment with prohibited medications (concurrent anticancer therapy including chemotherapy, radiation, hormonal treatment [except corticosteroids and megesterolacetate], or immunotherapy) =< 14 days prior to treatment with osimertinib

Any evidence of severe or uncontrolled systemic diseases, including uncontrolled hypertension and active bleeding diatheses, which in the investigator?s opinion makes it undesirable for the patient to participate in the trial or which would jeopardize compliance with the protocol, or known active infection including chronic active hepatitis B, hepatitis C and human immunodeficiency virus (HIV); screening for chronic conditions is not required; patients with chronic hepatitis B virus (HBV) with negative HBV viral load on appropriate antiviral therapy will be permitted, if able to continue appropriate antiviral therapy throughout treatment period
Active tuberculosis
Signs or symptoms of infection within 2 weeks prior to first day of study
Therapeutic oral or intravenous (IV) antibiotics within 2 weeks prior to first day of study treatment:
Class II to IV heart failure as defined by the New York Heart Association functional classification system

Patients with known coronary artery disease, congestive heart failure not meeting the above criteria, or left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF) < 50% must be on a stable medical regimen that is optimized in the opinion of the treating physician, in consultation with a cardiologist if appropriate, to be eligible

Patients who have experienced untreated and/or uncontrolled cardiovascular conditions and/or have symptomatic cardiac dysfunction (unstable angina, congestive heart failure, myocardial infarction within the previous 3 months; coronary angioplasty, or stenting or bypass grafting within the past 6 months; cardiac ventricular arrhythmias requiring medication; any history of second (2nd) or third (3rd) degree atrioventricular conduction defects)
pregnant
breastfeeding

Presence of active gastrointestinal (GI) disease (including GI bleeding or ulceration) or other condition that could affect GI absorption (e.g. malabsorption syndrome, history of biliary tract disease), including refractory nausea or vomiting, or chronic GI disease which may affect absorption or tolerance to oral medications
History of hypersensitivity to active or inactive excipients of osimertinib or drugs with a similar chemical structure or class to osimertinib
Involvement in the planning and/or conduct of the study (applies to both investigator staff and/or staff at the study site)
Participation in another clinical study with an investigational product during the last 2 months or within five half-lives of the compound, whichever is longer

Uncontrolled medical, psychological, familial, sociological, or geographical conditions that interfere with the patient?s safety, ability to provide informed consent, or ability to comply with the protocol

transcript.text: Hello, and thank you for your interest in the study "Osimertinib in Treating Participants With Stage I-IIIA EGFR-mutant Non-small Cell Lung Cancer Before Surgery". I'll ask you a short series of questions, one at a time. You can skip any question. A study coordinator will review everything you tell me and follow up with you.

transcript.speaker: agent
transcript.text: Thanks. Are you 18 years of age or older?

transcript.speaker: participant
transcript.text: Yes, I am 44 years old.

transcript.speaker: agent
transcript.text: Thanks. Have you had a biopsy to confirm your non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) diagnosis within the last 90 days? If you aren't sure of the exact date, that's okay.

transcript.speaker: participant
transcript.text: Yes, a biopsy confirmed my non-small cell lung cancer six weeks ago.

transcript.speaker: agent
transcript.text: Thanks. Have you had your tumor tested for an EGFR mutation (such as Exon 19 deletion, T790M, or L858R) using a CLIA-approved lab test? If you aren't sure, that's okay.

transcript.speaker: participant
transcript.text: I'm not sure about that. I don't know if my tumor was tested for an EGFR mutation or if the lab was CLIA-approved.

transcript.speaker: agent
transcript.text: Thanks. Have you received any treatment for your lung cancer in the last 28 days? If you aren't sure, that's okay.

transcript.speaker: participant
transcript.text: No, I haven't started any cancer treatment yet, of any kind.

transcript.speaker: agent
transcript.text: Thanks. Have you had any side effects from EGFR TKI treatment (a type of targeted cancer drug) that were moderate or severe (grade 2 or higher)? If you aren't sure, that's okay.

transcript.speaker: participant
transcript.text: I haven't had any side effects from EGFR TKI treatment because I haven't started any cancer treatment yet.

transcript.speaker: agent
transcript.text: Thanks. Have you had a PET-CT scan within the last 60 days to check the stage of your lung cancer? A PET-CT is a special imaging test that uses a small amount of radioactive material to show how organs and tissues are functioning.

transcript.speaker: participant

transcript.speaker: agent
transcript.text: To clarify, have you had a brain MRI (or a CT scan if an MRI isn't possible) within the last 60 days that showed no signs of cancer spreading to the brain? If you aren't sure, that's okay.

transcript.speaker: participant
transcript.text: I'm not sure about the specific dates of my recent imaging tests, so I don't know if I've had a brain MRI or CT scan within the last 60 days.

transcript.speaker: agent
transcript.text: Thanks. Have you been evaluated by a thoracic surgeon (a surgeon who specializes in chest and lung surgery) who is certified by the American Board of Thoracic Surgery and has determined that you are a candidate for lung cancer surgery? If you aren't sure, that's okay.

transcript.speaker: agent
transcript.text: Thanks. Do you know the size of your tumor in its longest dimension? The study requires the tumor to be at least 1 centimeter (about the size of a pea) in its longest diameter. If you aren't sure, that's okay.

transcript.speaker: participant
transcript.text: I don't know the exact size of my tumor. I haven't been given those specific details yet.

transcript.speaker: agent
transcript.text: Thanks. On a scale of 0 to 1, how would you describe your ability to carry out daily activities? transcript.speaker: participant
transcript.text: I would describe my ability to carry out daily activities as a 0. I am fully active.

transcript.speaker: agent
transcript.text: Hello, and thank you for your interest in the study "Osimertinib in Treating Participants With Stage I-IIIA EGFR-mutant Non-small Cell Lung Cancer Before Surgery". I'll ask you a short series of questions, one at a time. You can skip any question. A study coordinator will review everything you tell me and follow up with you.

transcript.speaker: agent
transcript.text: Thanks. Are you 18 years of age or older?

transcript.speaker: participant
transcript.text: Yes, I am 44 years old.

transcript.speaker: agent
transcript.text: Thanks. Have you had a biopsy to confirm your non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) diagnosis within the last 90 days? If you aren't sure of the exact date, that's okay.

transcript.speaker: participant
transcript.text: Yes, a biopsy confirmed my non-small cell lung cancer six weeks ago.

transcript.speaker: agent
transcript.text: Thanks. Have you had your tumor tested for an EGFR mutation (such as Exon 19 deletion, T790M, or L858R) using a CLIA-approved lab test? If you aren't sure, that's okay.

transcript.speaker: participant
transcript.text: I'm not sure about that. I don't know if my tumor was tested for an EGFR mutation or if the lab was CLIA-approved.

transcript.speaker: agent
transcript.text: Thanks. Have you received any treatment for your lung cancer in the last 28 days? If you aren't sure, that's okay.

transcript.speaker: participant
transcript.text: No, I haven't started any cancer treatment yet, of any kind.

transcript.speaker: agent
transcript.text: Thanks. Have you had any side effects from EGFR TKI treatment (a type of targeted cancer drug) that were moderate or severe (grade 2 or higher)? If you aren't sure, that's okay.

transcript.speaker: participant
transcript.text: I haven't had any side effects from EGFR TKI treatment because I haven't started any cancer treatment yet.

transcript.speaker: agent
transcript.text: Thanks. Have you had a PET-CT scan within the last 60 days to check the stage of your lung cancer? A PET-CT is a special imaging test that uses a small amount of radioactive material to show how organs and tissues are functioning.

transcript.speaker: participant
transcript.text: I don't know if I've had a PET-CT scan within the last 60 days. I'm not sure about the specific dates of my recent imaging tests.

transcript.speaker: agent
transcript.text: To clarify, have you had a brain MRI (or a CT scan if an MRI isn't possible) within the last 60 days that showed no signs of cancer spreading to the brain? If you aren't sure, that's okay.

transcript.speaker: participant
transcript.text: I'm not sure about the specific dates of my recent imaging tests, so I don't know if I've had a brain MRI or CT scan within the last 60 days.

transcript.speaker: agent
transcript.text: Thanks. Have you been evaluated by a thoracic surgeon (a surgeon who specializes in chest and lung surgery) who is certified by the American Board of Thoracic Surgery and has determined that you are a candidate for lung cancer surgery? If you aren't sure, that's okay.

transcript.speaker: participant
transcript.text: I haven't been evaluated by a thoracic surgeon yet. I'm not sure if I am a candidate for surgery.

transcript.speaker: agent
transcript.text: Thanks. Do you know the size of your tumor in its longest dimension? The study requires the tumor to be at least 1 centimeter (about the size of a pea) in its longest diameter. If you aren't sure, that's okay.

transcript.speaker: participant
transcript.text: I don't know the exact size of my tumor. I haven't been given those specific details yet.

transcript.speaker: agent
transcript.text: Thanks. On a scale of 0 to 1, how would you describe your ability to carry out daily activities? A score of 0 means you are fully active, and a score of 1 means you are restricted in physically strenuous activity but ambulatory and able to carry out light work. If you aren't sure, that's okay.

transcript.speaker: participant
transcript.text: I would describe my ability to carry out daily activities as a 0. I am fully active.

transcript.speaker: agent
transcript.text: Thanks. Are you able to swallow oral medications, such as pills or capsules?

transcript.speaker: participant
transcript.text: Yes, I can swallow oral medicines without any trouble.

transcript.speaker: agent
transcript.text: Thanks. Have you had a blood pregnancy test within the last 3 days? If you aren't sure, that's okay.

transcript.speaker: participant
transcript.text: Big tablets are a struggle for me, to be honest. I often can't get them down. So, no, I am not able to swallow oral medications without trouble.

transcript.speaker: agent
transcript.text: Thanks. Have you had a blood pregnancy test within the last 3 days? If you aren't sure, that's okay.

transcript.speaker: participant
transcript.text: No, I am not pregnant.

transcript.speaker: agent
transcript.text: Thanks. Are you willing to use a highly effective form of birth control during the study and for 90 days after your last dose of osimertinib?

transcript.speaker: participant
transcript.text: Yes, I'll use highly effective contraception throughout, and for the 90 days after the final dose.

transcript.speaker: agent
transcript.text: Thanks. Are you a man with a female partner who could become pregnant? If so, have you had a vasectomy or are you willing to use effective contraception for at least 14 days before the first dose, during the study, and for 90 days after the last dose?

transcript.speaker: participant
transcript.text: It asks about men, and I'm a woman, so I can't answer it.

transcript.speaker: agent
transcript.text: Thanks. Have you ever been diagnosed with leptomeningeal carcinomatosis (cancer spread to the lining of the brain and spinal cord) or other metastases in the central nervous system (CNS)?

transcript.speaker: participant
transcript.text: No, I have not been diagnosed with leptomeningeal carcinomatosis or other metastases in the central nervous system.

transcript.speaker: agent
transcript.text: Thanks. Have you been diagnosed with Stage IIIB lung cancer, or have you had distant metastases (cancer spread to other parts of the body) or malignant pleural effusion (fluid around the lungs containing cancer cells) identified on a PET-CT scan or biopsy?

transcript.speaker: participant
transcript.text: No, I have not been diagnosed with Stage IIIB lung cancer, nor have I had distant metastases or malignant pleural effusion.

transcript.speaker: agent
transcript.text: Thanks. Have you ever been diagnosed with interstitial lung disease (a condition causing scarring in the lungs), drug-induced interstitial lung disease, or radiation pneumonitis that required steroid treatment? Also, do you currently have any active symptoms related to these conditions?

transcript.speaker: participant
transcript.text: No, I have never been diagnosed with interstitial lung disease or radiation pneumonitis, and I don't have any active symptoms related to those conditions.

transcript.speaker: agent
transcript.text: Thanks. Have you ever tested positive for HIV (human immunodeficiency virus)?

transcript.speaker: participant
transcript.text: No, I have not tested positive for HIV. I've been tested and the result was negative.

transcript.speaker: agent
transcript.text: Thanks. Do you currently have any other active cancers besides the lung cancer we discussed?

transcript.speaker: participant
transcript.text: No, I do not have any other active cancers besides the lung cancer we discussed.

transcript.speaker: agent
transcript.text: Thanks. Are you currently taking any medications that might affect your heart rhythm (QTc prolonging) or strong liver enzyme inducers? If so, would it be possible to stop or switch these before the study starts?

transcript.speaker: participant
transcript.text: No, I don't take any regular medicines.

transcript.speaker: agent
transcript.text: Thanks. Have you ever had an electrocardiogram (ECG) that showed a prolonged QTc interval (greater than 470 msec)?

transcript.speaker: participant
transcript.text: I don't know if I've had an ECG showing a prolonged QTc interval. I'm not sure about the specific results of my past heart tests.

transcript.speaker: agent
transcript.text: Thanks. Have you ever been told by a doctor that you have a significant heart rhythm or conduction problem, such as a complete left bundle branch block or third-degree heart block?

transcript.speaker: participant
transcript.text: No, I have never been told by a doctor that I have a significant heart rhythm or conduction problem.

transcript.speaker: agent
transcript.text: Thanks. Have you ever been diagnosed with heart failure, or do you have a family history of long QT syndrome or unexplained sudden death in a close relative under age 40?

transcript.speaker: participant
transcript.text: No, I have never been diagnosed with heart failure, and I don't have a family history of long QT syndrome or unexplained sudden death.

transcript.speaker: agent
transcript.text: Thanks. Do you currently have any severe or uncontrolled health conditions, such as high blood pressure, active bleeding issues, or infections like hepatitis B, hepatitis C, or HIV?

transcript.speaker: participant
transcript.text: No, I don't have any severe or uncontrolled health conditions like high blood pressure, bleeding issues, or hepatitis.

transcript.speaker: agent
transcript.text: Thanks. Have you ever been diagnosed with active tuberculosis?

transcript.speaker: participant
transcript.text: No, I have never been diagnosed with active tuberculosis.

transcript.speaker: agent
transcript.text: Thanks. Have you had any signs or symptoms of an infection in the last 2 weeks, such as a fever, cough, or sore throat?

transcript.speaker: participant
transcript.text: No, I haven't had any signs or symptoms of an infection like a fever, cough, or sore throat in the last two weeks.

transcript.speaker: agent
transcript.text: Thanks. Have you taken any oral or IV antibiotics in the last 2 weeks? (IV antibiotics are given through a vein in your arm).

transcript.speaker: participant
transcript.text: No, I haven't taken any antibiotics for well over a year.

transcript.speaker: agent
transcript.text: Thanks. Do you have heart failure classified as Class II to IV by the New York Heart Association? This classification is based on how much physical activity causes symptoms like shortness of breath or fatigue.

transcript.speaker: participant
transcript.text: No, I have never been diagnosed with heart failure.

transcript.speaker: agent
transcript.text: Thanks. Do you have known coronary artery disease, or a left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF) below 50%? LVEF is a measurement of how well your heart pumps blood. If so, are you currently on a stable, optimized treatment plan for it?

transcript.speaker: participant
transcript.text: No, I do not have known coronary artery disease or a low ejection fraction. I don't take any regular medicines for heart conditions.

transcript.speaker: agent
transcript.text: Thanks. Have you had any of the following in the last 6 months: unstable chest pain (angina), a heart attack, a procedure to open a blocked heart artery (angioplasty or stenting), or heart bypass surgery?

transcript.speaker: participant
transcript.text: No, I have not had any of those heart issues in the last 6 months.

transcript.speaker: agent
transcript.text: Thanks. Are you currently breastfeeding?

transcript.speaker: participant
transcript.text: No, I am not breastfeeding.

transcript.speaker: agent
transcript.text: Thanks. Do you currently have any active stomach or intestinal issues, such as bleeding, ulcers, or conditions that affect how your body absorbs nutrients? Also, do you experience frequent nausea, vomiting, or have a chronic digestive condition that might make it hard to take oral medications?

transcript.speaker: participant
transcript.text: No, I don't have any active stomach or intestinal issues like bleeding or ulcers, and I don't have frequent nausea or vomiting.

transcript.speaker: agent
transcript.text: Thanks. Do you have any other conditions that might affect how your body absorbs nutrients, such as malabsorption syndrome or a history of gallbladder/bile duct issues? Or do you have a chronic digestive condition that makes it hard to take oral medications?

transcript.speaker: participant
transcript.text: No, I don't have any other conditions that affect nutrient absorption or chronic digestive issues that would make it hard to take oral medications.

transcript.speaker: agent
transcript.text: Thanks. Have you ever had an allergic reaction or hypersensitivity to osimertinib, any of its ingredients, or other drugs with a similar chemical structure?

transcript.speaker: participant
transcript.text: No, I have never had a hypersensitivity reaction to any drug, including osimertinib or similar medications.

transcript.speaker: agent
transcript.text: Thanks. Are you currently involved in the planning or conduct of this study, such as working as staff at the study site?

transcript.speaker: participant
transcript.text: No, I am not involved in the planning or conduct of this study. I work as a primary school teacher.

transcript.speaker: agent
transcript.text: To clarify, are you currently involved in the planning or conduct of this study, such as working as staff at the study site?

transcript.speaker: participant
transcript.text: No, I am not involved in the planning or conduct of this study. I teach at a primary school.

transcript.speaker: agent
transcript.text: Thanks. Have you taken part in any other clinical study involving an investigational product in the last 2 months?

transcript.speaker: participant
transcript.text: Yes, I took part in a migraine drug trial. I stopped taking the study medicine a month ago.

transcript.speaker: agent
transcript.text: Thanks. Do you have any medical, psychological, family, social, or location-related issues that might make it hard for you to stay safe, understand the study details, or follow the study schedule?

transcript.speaker: participant
transcript.text: No, I don't have any issues that would make it hard for me to stay safe or follow the study schedule.

transcript.speaker: agent
transcript.text: Thank you, that's all my questions. A study coordinator will review your answers and contact you about next steps.
